cards.q: What is the layer model for OSPF troubleshooting?
cards.a: OSPF troubleshooting follows: neighbor adjacency, then LSDB sync, then SPF, then route installation, then traffic. Most exam scenarios hang on neighbor-state issues (MTU, hello/dead, area, network type, auth) or area/type misconfiguration. Use a strict show-command progression to isolate the fault level.

cards.q: List the top-down OSPF troubleshooting flow with its commands.
cards.a: 1. Interface: is the link up? show ip interface brief. 2. Neighbor: adjacency formed? show ip ospf neighbor. 3. LSDB: databases synchronized? show ip ospf database. 4. Routes: SPF produced routes? show ip route ospf. 5. Forwarding: CEF has it? show ip cef or ping.

cards.q: Match each stuck OSPF neighbor state to its classic cause.
cards.a: Down: no hellos (link/ACL/multicast). Init: one-way hello visibility. 2-Way (no Full): DR/BDR election issue. ExStart: MTU mismatch. Exchange: DBD issue/MTU. Loading: LSA request unfulfilled.

cards.q: List the OSPF parameters that must match between neighbors.
cards.a: Hello/dead timers, area ID, network type (broadcast vs P2P), authentication type and key, MTU (else ExStart stuck), subnet/address family, and the stub flag (all routers in a stub/NSSA area must match).

cards.q: What is the fix for a neighbor stuck in ExStart due to MTU mismatch?
cards.a: Match the MTU on both sides or use ip ospf mtu-ignore. MTU mismatch is the single most-tested OSPF fault and the classic cause of ExStart stuck.

cards.q: What are the common OSPF operational issues and their fixes?
cards.a: Adjacency forms but no routes: LSDB not identical; check show ip ospf database. Routes flap: flapping interface or dead timer; tune hello/dead. External routes missing: stub area blocking Type 5; use NSSA or default. Cost unexpectedly equal: default reference 100 Mbps; set auto-cost reference-bandwidth. SPF storm/high CPU: area too big or flap; summarize + ISPF + throttle.

cards.q: What do the clear ip ospf commands do?
cards.a: clear ip ospf process resets neighbors and reconverges, causing a brief outage; clear ip ospf neighbor resets specific neighbor adjacencies; clear ip ospf counters clears counters. These are maintenance actions, not configuration fixes.

cards.q: What command triggers an adjacency when a neighbor is stuck?
cards.a: debug ip ospf adjacency (or debug ip ospf events) can reveal why, but must be used carefully in production. The stuck-state commands include show ip ospf neighbor detail and show ip ospf interface.

cards.q: What is the single most-tested OSPF fault?
cards.a: MTU mismatch, which causes a neighbor stuck in ExStart. This is the memorized answer for the classic neighbor-stuck-in-ExStart scenario.

cards.q: What must match on all routers in a stub or NSSA area or adjacencies fail?
cards.a: The stub flag (area type). All routers in a stub/NSSA area must have the same stub/NSSA configuration or adjacencies will fail to form.

cards.q: What neighbor state does a hello/dead timer or auth mismatch cause?
cards.a: Hello/dead mismatch causes a neighbor stuck in Init or Down, never Full. An authentication mismatch also causes a neighbor stuck in Init.

cards.q: Why is clear ip ospf process not a configuration fix?
cards.a: Because it only reconverges the OSPF process (resets neighbors and rebuilds adjacencies with a brief outage). It does not fix the underlying configuration problem that caused the fault.

cards.q: Match each OSPF fault to its remedy.
cards.a: MTU mismatch to ExStart, fix by matching MTU or mtu-ignore; hello/dead mismatch to Down/Init, fix by matching timers; auth mismatch to Init, fix by matching type and key; network type mismatch to neighbor issues; stub flag mismatch to no adjacency; DR issue to 2-Way stuck, fix with priorities or point-to-point; external blocked to missing routes, fix with area type or NSSA; SPF storm to high CPU, fix with summarize plus ISPF.
